findings.evidence: The requester gets an automatic reminder after three days.
findings.violation: The document names the single person requesting the stipend with at least four different terms across separate sections: employees and the employee in Eligibility and How to Apply, the applicant in Restrictions and Exceptions, the requester here in Approval Timeline, and you in Terminology Notes, with no defined-terms section or stated equivalence signaling they name the same person, so a reader following the process across sections cannot be certain the requester and the applicant are the same party the rest of the document calls the employee.
findings.fix: Pick one term, for example you, and use it consistently for the person requesting the stipend in every section.

instances.evidence: Full-time employees who have completed 90 days of continuous service are eligible for the home-office equipment stipend.
Also, you submit the request in the portal.

findings.evidence: 71-word sentence, 5 subordinate-clause markers: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 71 words with 5 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.

findings.evidence: The determination of stipend eligibility happens before any payment goes out. The escalation of repeat requests happens automatically within the same quarter.
findings.violation: Both sentences in this section route their action through an abstract nominalized subject, the determination and the escalation, rather than naming the office or role that actually determines eligibility or escalates a repeat request; no actor is named anywhere in the section, so the reader cannot tell who is responsible for either action.
findings.fix: Name the actual actor as the subject of each sentence, for example: the benefits team determines eligibility before releasing payment, and the benefits team escalates repeat requests automatically within the same quarter.

findings.evidence: 71-word sentence: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.violation: At 71 words, with 0 comma-set-off clause(s) and 5 subordinate-clause marker(s), the sentence stacks interruptions between its subject and its main verb instead of holding the main clause together.
findings.fix: Move subordinate clauses and modifiers after the main clause, not between its subject and verb.

findings.evidence: The finance liaison reviews the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year.
findings.violation: Three separate sections state, in nearly identical wording, that a different office reviews or tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year: the benefits team in Program Overview, the finance liaison here in Special Cases, and the people operations office in Questions and Updates, with nothing signaling whether these are three names for one office or three offices genuinely doing the same task, so a reader cannot tell which office actually owns the budget.
findings.fix: State the budget-tracking fact once, name the one office responsible, and remove the near-duplicate restatements from Special Cases and Questions and Updates.

instances.evidence: The benefits team tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year.
The people operations office tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year.

findings.evidence: Employees must submit the receipt, the manager's approval form, and the original purchase order before the review begins.
findings.violation: The sentence embeds three or more comma- or semicolon-separated parallel items inline rather than presenting them as a formatted list.
findings.fix: Reformat the inline items as a numbered or bulleted list.

findings.evidence: Additionally, employees shall retain receipts for one year after the purchase date.
findings.violation: The sentence states a binding requirement using shall or an indirect requirement phrasing instead of must.

findings.evidence: The finance office conducts an evaluation of every submitted receipt before it approves the amount.
findings.violation: The action is buried inside the noun 'evaluation', carried by a generic support verb, instead of stated as the sentence's own main verb.
findings.fix: Restate the nominalized noun as the sentence's main verb.

findings.evidence: Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt.
findings.violation: This section states the request's step sequence, information the reader needs before or alongside How to Apply, but it appears after Approval Timeline, Required Documentation, Reimbursement Amounts, Restrictions and Exceptions, and Terminology Notes instead, sections that presuppose the request is already under way, so the ordering tracks how the document was assembled rather than the reader's actual task sequence.
findings.fix: Move Request Steps immediately after How to Apply, or merge its content into that section.
